activities.title: Binary numbers
activities.description: Fifteen questions on binary representation: place value, conversion to and from decimal and hexadecimal, two's complement, binary arithmetic, bitwise operators and shifts. Written for Leaving Certificate Computer Science.

config.title: Binary numbers
config.instructions: Work each one out on paper before you choose. Every question tells you how many marks it is worth.

questions.stem: What is the binary number 10110110 in denary (base 10)?
What is the denary number 200 as an 8-bit binary number?
How many different values can be represented using 12 bits?
What is the largest number that can be stored in one unsigned byte?
How is −40 represented in 8-bit two's complement?
What range of whole numbers can be represented in 8-bit two's complement?
Add these two 8-bit binary numbers. What is the result?
What is the hexadecimal number 2F as an 8-bit binary number?
What is the binary number 11011010 in hexadecimal?
An unsigned binary number is shifted one place to the left, with a 0 put into the empty place on the right. Assuming no bit is lost off the left-hand end, what happens to its value?
What is the result of the bitwise AND of these two bytes?
Which of these 8-bit two's complement numbers represent NEGATIVE values? Choose all that apply.
A school needs to give every one of its 1000 students a different binary code. What is the smallest number of bits that will do?
An image stores each pixel using 8 bits for red, 8 bits for green and 8 bits for blue. How many different colours can one pixel be?
Why do computers represent data in binary rather than in denary?

options.text: A binary number always needs fewer digits than the same denary number.
Binary uses less memory than denary.
Electronic components can reliably tell two states apart, so two symbols are far less error-prone than ten.
Arithmetic can only be carried out in binary.

q1.explanation: Write the place values above the bits: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. The 1s sit under 128, 32, 16, 4 and 2, and 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182.

q2.explanation: Take the largest place value that fits and keep going: 200 − 128 = 72, 72 − 64 = 8, 8 − 8 = 0. So the 128, 64 and 8 columns hold a 1 and the rest hold 0: 11001000.

q3.explanation: Each extra bit doubles the number of patterns, so n bits give 2^n of them. 2^12 = 4096. Note 4096 is the count of values, not the largest one — the largest is 4095, because the count starts at 0.

q4.explanation: A byte is 8 bits, giving 2^8 = 256 patterns. They run from 0 to 255, so the largest is 255 — one less than the number of patterns, because 0 uses one of them.

q5.explanation: Start with +40 = 00101000. Invert every bit to get 11010111, then add 1 to get 11011000. (Check it: 256 − 40 = 216, and 11011000 is 128 + 64 + 16 + 8 = 216.) 11010111 is the one's complement — a common slip, because it stops one step early.

q6.explanation: The 256 patterns are split unevenly: 128 of them for negatives (−128 to −1) and 128 for zero and the positives (0 to 127). Zero takes one of the positive side's places, which is why the range reaches −128 but only +127.

q7.explanation: 01101101 is 109 and 00010110 is 22, so the answer is 131 = 10000011. Working in binary, the carries ripple through the run of 1s in the middle — 01111011 is what you get if you drop one of them.

q8.explanation: Each hex digit is exactly four bits, so convert them separately: 2 = 0010 and F = 1111. Join them: 00101111. This is why hex is used as shorthand for binary — no arithmetic is needed, just a lookup.

q9.explanation: Split the byte into nibbles: 1101 and 1010. 1101 = 13 = D, 1010 = 10 = A. So the answer is DA. AD is the same two digits the wrong way round.

q10.explanation: Every bit moves into a column worth twice as much, so the value doubles — exactly as adding a 0 to the right of a denary number multiplies it by 10. Shifting right one place halves it, discarding any remainder.

q11.explanation: AND gives 1 only where BOTH bits are 1. Comparing column by column leaves 01001000. The other two answers are the traps: 11101110 is OR (1 where EITHER is 1) and 10100110 is XOR (1 where they DIFFER).

q12.explanation: In two's complement the leftmost bit is the sign bit: 1 means negative. So 10000000 (−128), 11111111 (−1) and 10101010 (−86) are negative, while 01111111 (+127) and 00000001 (+1) are positive. You do not need to work out the values — the first bit is enough.

q13.explanation: 9 bits give 2^9 = 512 codes, which is not enough for 1000 students. 10 bits give 2^10 = 1024, which is. So 10 is the smallest that works — with 24 codes to spare.

q14.explanation: The three channels are independent, so the totals multiply rather than add: 256 × 256 × 256 = 2^24 = 16 777 216. That is the same as treating the whole pixel as one 24-bit number. 768 is what you get by adding the channels instead of multiplying.

q15.explanation: A circuit only has to tell 'voltage present' from 'voltage absent', and that decision survives noise, heat and ageing components. Ten distinguishable voltage levels would be far more fragile. Binary actually needs MORE digits than denary, not fewer — reliability is worth that cost.
